entry.title: Giving a Great Talk
entry.content:
Robert Spekkens’ PIRSA talk Tips for giving a great talk is the kind of resource I like because it treats scientific speaking as a craft. A good talk is not simply a compressed paper, nor a display of how much the speaker knows. It is an act of communication shaped around an audience.

The central discipline, I think, is selection. A talk has to decide what it is really about: the one question, distinction, example, or result that should remain with the listener afterwards. Many talks fail not because the material is weak, but because the speaker tries to preserve too much of the paper’s internal architecture.

This is especially important in foundational and philosophical work, where confusion can easily arise from terms that are familiar but used differently by different communities. A good talk should not merely state definitions; it should help the audience feel why the distinctions matter.

The best talks often leave me with a clearer question, not only with more information. That is a useful standard to aim for.

Source: Robert Spekkens, Tips for giving a great talk, Perimeter Institute, October 17, 2022. DOI: 10.48660/22100109.
entry.summary: A note on clarity, audience, and the craft of scientific presentations.

entry.title: Finding Your Element
entry.content:
Ken Robinson’s Finding Your Element: How to Discover Your Talents and Passions and Transform Your Life is a practical companion to his broader idea of “the element”: the point where what one is good at and what one cares about begin to reinforce each other.

I am interested in this less as a self-help formula than as an educational question. Many people are asked to make life-shaping decisions before they have had enough space to encounter different kinds of work, different communities, and different versions of themselves. In that setting, “finding one’s element” is not a matter of introspection alone. It requires experiments, teachers, environments, and chances to discover what forms of attention feel alive.

The idea also connects to academic work. Research becomes more sustainable when ability and interest are not pulled apart too violently. One can endure difficulty, boredom, and frustration much better when the underlying question still feels like one’s own.

The danger, of course, is to romanticise fit as something immediate or pure. Sometimes one discovers one’s element only by working through resistance. But the basic thought remains important: education should not merely sort people by performance; it should help them notice where their capacities and concerns can genuinely meet.

Source: Ken Robinson and Lou Aronica, Finding Your Element: How to Discover Your Talents and Passions and Transform Your Life.
entry.summary: A reading note on talent, passion, education, and finding work that fits.

entry.title: Von Neumann and Myths of Genius

link.title: Von Neumann and Myths of Genius

entry.content:
Erik Hoel’s essay John von Neumann Shot Lightning From His Arse is partly a myth-checking exercise and partly a reflection on how stories about genius get used. Von Neumann was plainly extraordinary; the interesting question is what follows from that fact, and what does not.

I find this useful because anecdotes about exceptional people often become too clean. They are used to support broad claims about innate ability, education, culture, discipline, or social environment, while the historical person disappears behind the lesson one wants to draw.

For education, the more productive question is not whether genius is real. It is how talent, training, opportunity, taste, ambition, and institutional context interact. Myths of effortless brilliance can be demoralising because they hide the ecology of development: teachers, books, conversations, expectations, and the concrete habits through which ability becomes work.

There is also a lesson for intellectual humility. Even great minds are not magic explanations. They are people situated in traditions, collaborations, rivalries, and accidents of timing.

Source: Erik Hoel, John von Neumann Shot Lightning From His Arse.
entry.summary: A reading note on genius, education, anecdotes, and the stories we tell about exceptional minds.

entry.title: Risk and Scientific Work
entry.content:
George Musser’s FQxI article Risky Business: How Science Plays Things Too Safe describes a familiar tension in academic life. Science celebrates boldness in retrospect, but often rewards caution in advance. Funding, hiring, publishing, and peer evaluation all tend to favor projects that are legible, feasible, and likely to produce visible output.

The uncomfortable part is that this is not simply the fault of one villainous institution. Researchers, journals, funders, and departments all participate in the same incentive structure. Risk is admired when it succeeds, but failure remains difficult to narrate professionally.

This seems especially relevant for foundational work. Some questions are slow, conceptually awkward, and difficult to package as guaranteed deliverables. But if science only supports paths whose value is already obvious, it risks selecting against precisely the forms of inquiry that could change the background picture.

The difficult ideal is not risk for its own sake. It is risk with standards: speculative enough to matter, rigorous enough to deserve trust.

Source: George Musser, Risky Business: How Science Plays Things Too Safe.
entry.summary: A reading note on why science often rewards safety even while admiring risk.

entry.title: Reality Keeps Unfolding
entry.content:
I want to return to the thought in Reality just keeps unfolding, from The Imperfectionist. Even the title captures something I find intellectually healthy: reality is not a closed object we simply possess once the right theory is written down, but something we continue to meet through inquiry, experiment, interpretation, and revision.

This attitude matters in physics and philosophy. It leaves room for formal precision without turning precision into premature finality. A theory can be extraordinarily successful and still leave us with questions about what is being represented, what counts as observation, and how the agent who uses the theory fits into the story.

For me, the useful lesson is not skepticism for its own sake, but a disciplined openness. One can take theories seriously while resisting the temptation to treat current conceptual pictures as the last possible word.

Source: Reality just keeps unfolding.
entry.summary: A short note on openness, incompleteness, and the difficulty of final interpretations.

entry.title: On Enjoying One’s Work
entry.content:
I recently returned to Terence Tao’s short note Enjoy your work. Its central reminder is simple but easy to lose sight of: serious intellectual work requires sustained effort, and sustained effort is much easier to give when one’s motivation is tied to real sources of satisfaction rather than rare external rewards.

For research, this seems especially important. There are many temptations to outsource one’s sense of direction: fashion, prestige, visible productivity, or the hope of a decisive breakthrough. But most days of research are not breakthrough days. They are days of trying to understand a small point more clearly, reformulating a question, noticing that an argument does not quite work, or helping someone else see a structure that had been obscure.

Those smaller forms of progress are not merely consolation prizes. They are often the actual substance of the work. A healthy intellectual life needs taste, patience, and contact with questions that feel worth returning to even when no immediate result is in view.

This is also one reason I find conversations, seminars, and good expository writing so valuable. They can remind us that research is not only a race for outcomes, but also a way of keeping alive certain forms of attention.

Source: Terence Tao, Enjoy your work.
entry.summary: A short reading note on work, patience, and realistic sources of satisfaction.
